metadata.scope: e_anatolia (20 non-867 baronies across k_anatolia and k_georgia; excludes baronies where is_historical_at['867'] is true)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}; all entries here have '867': false.
schema_notes.replacement_candidates: List of exactly 3 associated natural feature names and historical tribal/ethnonym names (>=1 tribe per barony) usable as localisation replacements.
schema_notes.name: Clean display name of the replacement candidate (Wikipedia disambiguation suffixes extracted to disambiguation_note).
schema_notes.disambiguation_note: Optional disambiguator extracted from parenthetical/comma qualifiers (e.g. 'Liao', 'Orkney', 'river'); null if none.
schema_notes.localisation_stem: Clean CK3-ready toponym stem stripped of redundant generic English feature suffixes/prefixes ('River', 'Mount', 'Lake', 'people', etc.) while preserving meaningful compounds.
schema_notes.attestation_basis: Historicity classification distinguishing genuinely pre-867/pre-literate entities from medieval post-867 ethnogeneses: attested_pre_867 | indigenous_pre_literate | attested_867_to_1066 | attested_1066_to_1178.
schema_notes.valid_for_bookmarks: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'} indicating whether the replacement candidate is historically non-anachronistic for that bookmark (true for both attested_pre_867 and indigenous_pre_literate; bookmark-gated for attested_867_to_1066 and attested_1066_to_1178).
schema_notes.candidates_with_multilingual_variants: Count of replacement candidates having more than 1 distinct language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 or documented proto-stage code) across language_variants.
schema_notes.language_variants_policy: Include core local/classical forms plus regionally scoped vernaculars and genuinely distinct exonyms; exclude out-of-region exonym padding and redundant eng copies (eng is retained only when no non-English variant exists). Uses ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 language_code values plus documented Wiktionary proto/stage codes (sla-pro, gem-pro, cel-pro, cel-bry, urj-fin-pro); reconstructed proto/ancient forms carry a leading '*'.
schema_notes.language_variants: List of cultural/historical name forms: {form, native_script, language, language_code, notes}. form is always clean Latin script (or romanization) suitable for CK3 localisation; native_script holds the native non-Latin script form or null when the language natively uses Latin script.
schema_notes.relationship: Prose description of the geographical, ecological, or historical relationship between the replacement entity and the audited barony.
schema_notes.etymology_notes: Linguistic etymology, onomastic origin, or geographic/ethnographic characterization of the replacement entity (incorporating attested onomastic notes from language variants where documented).

replacement_candidates.name: Luwians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Bronze Age Anatolian inhabitants of southern Anatolia including Rough Cilicia and Isauria.

language_variants.notes: Hittite adverbial designation for Luwian-speaking lands

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1600 BCE (Hittite Old Kingdom texts from Hattusa)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Indo-European Anatolian ethnonym attested in Hittite cuneiform as Luwili / Luwiya.

replacement_candidates.name: Göksu
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river flowing through Isauria and Rough Cilicia to the Mediterranean.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 400 BCE (classical Greek geographical sources as Kalykadnos)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Turkish Göksu ('sky-blue water'); classical Kalykadnos of uncertain Anatolian origin.

replacement_candidates.name: Taurus Mountains
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major mountain range dominating Isauria.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Classical Greek geography (Xenophon, Strabo) from the 4th–1st century BCE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Ancient Greek Tauros ('bull'), possibly from Semitic or Anatolian root for mountain.

replacement_candidates.name: Solymoi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient indigenous people of southwestern Anatolia in the Pisidia-Lycia borderlands.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 750 BCE (Homer, Iliad 6.184)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Pre-Greek Anatolian ethnonym recorded by Homer and Strabo in the mountains of Pisidia and Lycia.

replacement_candidates.name: Lake Burdur
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large tectonic saline lake in Pisidia near the Yeşilova basin.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 100 BCE (Strabo, Geography, as Lake Ascania)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Turkish Burdur Gölü; identified with classical Lake Ascania in Pisidia.

replacement_candidates.name: Paroreios Phrygia
replacement_candidates.relationship: Classical Greek and Roman name for the mountain-lined Pisidian-Phrygian borderland along the Sultan Dağları.

language_variants.notes: Strabo's Greek name ('Phrygia by the Mountains')

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Strabo (Geographica, c. 20 BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Classical Greek Parṓreios ('beside the mountain range'), predating Seljuk Sultan Dağları.

replacement_candidates.name: Hittites
replacement_candidates.relationship: Bronze Age Anatolian people who ruled central and eastern Anatolia including Cataonia.

language_variants.notes: Endonym for the Hittite language ('of Neša')

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1650 BCE (Hittite Old Kingdom royal annals from Hattusa)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from the Bronze Age land of Hatti in central Anatolia.

replacement_candidates.name: Ceyhan River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river rising in the Elbistan-Lykandos basin and flowing to the Mediterranean.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 401 BCE (Xenophon, Anabasis 1.4.1, as Pyramus)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Ancient Pyramus; medieval Arabic Jayhan, whence Turkish Ceyhan.

replacement_candidates.name: Anti-Taurus Mountains
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range framing the Lykandos and Cataonia basin in eastern Anatolia.

language_variants.notes: Modern Turkish name for the main range

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 100 BCE (Strabo, Geography, as Antitauros)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Greek Antitauros ('opposite the Taurus'), describing the northern parallel range.

replacement_candidates.name: Hurrians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Bronze Age people of Kizzuwatna and Cilicia.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 2200 BCE (Akkadian and Hurrian cuneiform inscriptions)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in Mesopotamian and Hittite cuneiform as Hurri / Hurrite.

replacement_candidates.name: Gulf of Alexandretta
replacement_candidates.relationship: Northeasternmost bay of the Mediterranean Sea where Ayas (Aegeae) is situated.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 333 BCE (classical accounts of the Battle of Issus, as Issic Gulf)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after ancient Issus (Sinus Issicus) and later Alexandretta (İskenderun).

replacement_candidates.name: Nur Mountains
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient Mount Amanus separating Cilicia from northern Syria along the Gulf of Alexandretta.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Khamanu in Assyrian annals (9th century BCE) and Amanos in Strabo (1st century CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Ancient Amanus (possibly Semitic/Hurrian origin); Turkish Nur Dağları ('Mountains of Light').

replacement_candidates.name: Svans
replacement_candidates.relationship: Kartvelian ethnic subgroup indigenous to Upper Svaneti around Mestia (Seti).
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 20 CE (Strabo, Geography 11.2.19, as Soanes)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Endonym Shwanär / Georgian Svanebi; attested by Strabo as Soanes.

replacement_candidates.name: Enguri
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river flowing from Upper Svaneti past Mestia (Seti) to the Black Sea.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Georgian and European travelers' records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Kartvelian hydronym; Georgian Enguri, Mingrelian Ingiri.

replacement_candidates.name: Ushba
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent twin-peaked mountain towering above Mestia (Seti) in Upper Svaneti.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (traditional Svan toponymy recorded in early modern sources)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Svan, traditionally glossed as 'Sabbath of the storm' or 'terrible mountain'.

replacement_candidates.name: Mingrelians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Kartvelian ethnic subgroup indigenous to Samegrelo (Odishi) around Zugdidi.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 12th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles of Samegrelo/Egrisi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Egrisi / Margali, the historical Kartvelian designation for Mingrelia.

replacement_candidates.name: Khobi
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing through Samegrelo (Odishi) near Zugdidi into the Black Sea.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 131 CE (Arrian, Periplus of the Euxine Sea, as Chobos)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in classical periploi as Chobos / Chobus; Georgian Khobistsqali.

replacement_candidates.name: Colchis
replacement_candidates.relationship: Classical historical region of western Georgia encompassing Samegrelo.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 750 BCE (Urartian inscriptions as Qulha; Greek Eumelus/Herodotus)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Urartian Qulha, rendered in Ancient Greek as Kolchis.

replacement_candidates.name: Heniochi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient tribe inhabiting the northwestern Caucasus and Colchian highlands.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 400 BCE (Pseudo-Scylax and classical Greek periploi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Greek Heniochoi ('charioteers'), likely a Greek folk-etymological adaptation of a local ethnonym.

replacement_candidates.name: Tskhenistsqali
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing directly past Tsageri through Lechkhumi into the Rioni.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 131 CE (Arrian, Periplus of the Euxine Sea, as Hippos)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Tskhenis-tsqali ('horse water'), translated into Ancient Greek as Hippos. Onomastic note: Ancient Greek 'Híppos' (Classical Greek calque (Hippos)).

replacement_candidates.name: Lechkhumi Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range rising above Tsageri in Lechkhumi.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Georgian geographical records of Lechkhumi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the historical Georgian province of Lechkhumi (medieval Takveri).

replacement_candidates.name: Abkhazians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Northwest Caucasian ethnic group giving its name to the duchy of Abkhazia.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 131 CE (Arrian, Periplus of the Euxine Sea, as Abasgoi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Apkhazebi, related to classical Abasgoi / Abasgi; endonym Apswaa.

replacement_candidates.name: Rioni
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river of western Georgia flowing through Ambrolauri in Racha.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 700 BCE (Hesiod, Theogony 340, as Phasis)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Ancient Phasis; medieval Georgian Rioni, from an indigenous Caucasian hydronym.

replacement_candidates.name: Racha Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range bordering the upper Rioni valley and Ambrolauri.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles mentioning Racha)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the historical highland province of Racha in western Georgia.

replacement_candidates.name: Apsilae
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient and early medieval people of the western Caucasus and Abkhazia.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 77 CE (Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.4, as Absilae)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in Pliny and Arrian; cognate with Abkhaz endonym Apswa.

replacement_candidates.name: Kodori
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river of Abkhazia draining the western Greater Caucasus.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Caucasian geographical records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Indigenous Abkhaz-Georgian hydronym (Abkhaz Kwydry, Georgian Kodori).

replacement_candidates.name: Tetnuldi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent snow-capped peak in the central Greater Caucasus of Svaneti.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (traditional Svan toponymy)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Svan meaning 'White Mountain' (cf. Georgian tetri 'white').

replacement_candidates.name: Legae
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient Northeast Caucasian tribe recorded near the eastern Greater Caucasus and Albania.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in Strabo's Geography (early 1st century CE) and Plutarch as a people of eastern Caucasian Albania.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Classical Legai/Legae, corresponding to Georgian Lekebi for Dagestani/Lezgic peoples.

replacement_candidates.name: Alazani
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river of Kakheti and Hereti flowing near Zaqatala.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 20 CE (Strabo, Geography 11.3.2, as Alazonios)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in Strabo and Pliny as Alazonius; Georgian Alazani.

replacement_candidates.name: Greater Caucasus
replacement_candidates.relationship: Main mountain range of the Caucasus rising immediately north of Zaqatala.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 470 BCE (Aeschylus and Herodotus, as Kaukasos)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Classical Kaukasos, possibly from a Scythian or Caucasian root meaning 'ice-shining' or 'white-peak'.

replacement_candidates.name: Kakhetians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ethnographic subgroup of Georgians inhabiting Kakheti and Hereti.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 8th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles of Kakheti)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from the historical region of Kakheti (earlier Kakha / Kukheti).

replacement_candidates.name: Iori
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing through Kakheti and the Dedoplistsqaro steppe into the Mingachevir basin.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 20 CE (Strabo, Geography 11.4.1, as Cambyses)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Identified with classical Cambyses; Georgian Iori.

replacement_candidates.name: Tsiv-Gombori Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range in Kakheti separating the Alazani and Iori valleys.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Georgian geographical records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of Georgian Tsivi ('cold') and Gombori, a local toponym.

replacement_candidates.name: Udi people
replacement_candidates.relationship: Indigenous Lezgic people of the Shaki-Hereti region, descendants of the classical Utii.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 440 BCE (Herodotus, Histories 3.93, as Utioi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested by Herodotus and Strabo as Utioi / Utians; endonym Udi.

replacement_candidates.name: Kura
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river of the eastern South Caucasus basin.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 100 BCE (Strabo and Plutarch, as Kyros / Cyrus)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Classical Kyros / Cyrus; Georgian Mtkvari ('slow' or 'good water').

replacement_candidates.name: Mount Bazardüzü
replacement_candidates.relationship: Highest peak of the eastern Greater Caucasus near the Shaki-Hereti frontier.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Azerbaijani and Lezgian toponymy)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Azerbaijani Bazardüzü ('market flat/plain'); Lezgian Kichen suv ('mountain of fear').

replacement_candidates.name: Armenians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Indigenous people of the Armenian Highlands including Gugark and Lori.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Armina in the Behistun Inscription of Darius I (520 BCE) and in Hecataeus/Herodotus.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Exonym from Old Persian Armina; endonym Hayk/Hayer.

replacement_candidates.name: Debed
replacement_candidates.relationship: Main river of the Lori region flowing north into Georgia.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 10th century CE (medieval Armenian and Georgian chronicles)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Medieval Armenian Debed / Georgian Debeda.

replacement_candidates.name: Dzoraget
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river of Lori flowing through a deep gorge to join the Pambak and form the Debed.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Armenian regional toponymy)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Armenian Dzoraget, compound of dzor ('gorge') and get ('river').

replacement_candidates.name: Saspeires
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient people of the South Caucasus and northeastern Anatolia attested by Herodotus.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 440 BCE (Herodotus, Histories 3.94, as Saspeires)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in Herodotus between Media and Colchis; linked by scholars to early Iberians/Sper.

replacement_candidates.name: Aghstev
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing through northern Armenia near Kayan into the Kura basin.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 13th century CE (medieval Armenian and Caucasian chronicles)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Armenian Aghstev; Azerbaijani Ağstafaçay.

replacement_candidates.name: Pambak
replacement_candidates.relationship: River in northern Armenia joining the Dzoraget to form the Debed.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Armenian geographical records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Traditional Armenian hydronym for the upper Debed tributary.

replacement_candidates.name: Alans
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iranic nomadic people of the Caucasus whose descendants settled in Shida Kartli.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1st century CE (Seneca, Lucan, Josephus, and Chinese Hou Hanshu)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Iranian *Aryana ('Aryan').

replacement_candidates.name: Great Liakhvi
replacement_candidates.relationship: River rising in the Greater Caucasus and flowing directly through Tskhinvali.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Didi Liakhvi ('Great Liakhvi'); Ossetian Styr Lewakhi.

replacement_candidates.name: Trialeti Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range bordering Shida Kartli to the south.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles mentioning Trialeti)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the historical Georgian district of Trialeti.

replacement_candidates.name: Georgians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Kartvelian people of Kartli and the central South Caucasus.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles as Kartveli; Latin/Greek Georgia)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Endonym Kartveli (from Kartli); exonym Georgians via Persian Gurj / Greek Georgios.

replacement_candidates.name: Tedzami
replacement_candidates.relationship: Right tributary of the Kura flowing through Shida Kartli near Gori.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Georgian geographical records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian hydronym for the river draining the northern Trialeti slopes.

replacement_candidates.name: Likhi Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range separating eastern and western Georgia on the western edge of Shida Kartli.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles, also Surami Range)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Likhis kedi, named after the Likhi pass and district.

replacement_candidates.name: Meskhetians
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ethnographic subgroup of Georgians indigenous to Samtskhe and Javakheti.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 440 BCE (Herodotus, Histories 3.94, as Moschoi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Meskhebi, linked to classical Moschoi.

replacement_candidates.name: Paravani Lake
replacement_candidates.relationship: Largest lake in Georgia, situated on the Javakheti Plateau.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Paravnis tba / Armenian Parvana.

replacement_candidates.name: Javakheti Plateau
replacement_candidates.relationship: Volcanic plateau in southern Georgia traversed by the upper Kura near Tmogvi.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 785 BCE (Urartian inscriptions of Argishti I as Zabakha)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Urartian Zabakha, whence Georgian Javakheti and Armenian Javakhk.

replacement_candidates.name: Mushki
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iron Age people of eastern Anatolia and the southern Caucasus borderlands.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1114 BCE (Assyrian inscriptions of Tiglath-Pileser I)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in Assyrian annals as Muški; often connected with classical Moschoi.

replacement_candidates.name: Meskheti Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range bordering Samtskhe and Akhaltsikhe to the north.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles of Meskheti)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the historical Georgian region of Meskheti.

replacement_candidates.name: Samsari Range
replacement_candidates.relationship: Volcanic mountain range in Samtskhe-Javakheti.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Georgian geographical records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Samsris kedi, named after Mount Didi Abuli and Samsari.

replacement_candidates.name: Taochi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient people of Tao in northeastern Anatolia attested by Xenophon.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 401 BCE (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.7.1, as Taochoi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Related to Urartian Diauehi / Daiaeni; Armenian Tayk and Georgian Tao.

replacement_candidates.name: Çoruh
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river of northeastern Anatolia and Tao-Klarjeti flowing into the Black Sea.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 6th century CE (Procopius, as Boas / Akampsis; medieval Georgian Chorokhi)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Kartvelian/Armenian Chorokhi, Turkish Çoruh.

replacement_candidates.name: Kaçkar Mountains
replacement_candidates.relationship: High mountain range rising northwest of Tortum in the eastern Pontic Alps.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 17th century CE (early modern Armenian and Ottoman records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Armenian Kajkar ('brave stone' / 'cross-stone').

replacement_candidates.name: Chalybes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient iron-working people of northeastern Anatolia and the Pontic-Caucasian borderlands.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 5th century BCE (Herodotus and Xenophon, Anabasis)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Ancient Greek Chalybes, associated with early metallurgy and Byzantine Chaldia.

replacement_candidates.name: Yalnızçam Mountains
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain range (Arsiani Range) along the Tao-Ardahan watershed.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 11th century CE (medieval Georgian chronicles as Arsiani)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Georgian Arsiani; Turkish Yalnızçam ('lone pine').

replacement_candidates.name: Lesser Caucasus
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain system spanning northeastern Anatolia and southern Georgia.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: The Caucasus system is attested in Aeschylus and Herodotus (5th century BCE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Southern branch of the Caucasus mountain system.
